detail.longDescription: Is it possible to decorate a function with a class decorator with arguments using the @decorator syntax? Note : Our class needs to store the function. Therefore we pass it in the __init__ method. The example below has been reduced to show only the important things. import functools class decorator_class: def __init__(self, func, *args0, **kwargs0): self.func = func # <- note: we need the function in the class self.args0 = args0 self.kwargs0 = kwargs0 functools.update_wrapper(self, func) def __call__(self, *args, **kwargs): print(self.func.__name__, self.args0, self.kwargs0, args, kwargs) return self.func(*args, **kwargs) # @decorator_class("arg", key="value") # <- this is not working def f(*args, **kwargs): # do something print("f", args, kwargs) f = decorator_class(f, "decorator arg", decorator_kwarg="value") # <- this works f("some_arg", some_kwarg="some_value") This decorator class works fine as decorator with arguments when using following syntax: f = decorator_class(f, "decorator arg", decorator_kwarg="value") But not with the @decorator syntax: # @decorator_class("arg", key="value") # <- this is not working When used with the @decorator syntax the __init__ method gets the first argument "arg" passed to its func argument. What do I miss here?
